[THOUGHT]  
The clinical summary presents a classic, high-probability case of Essential Thrombocythemia (ET), a clonal Philadelphia chromosome–negative myeloproliferative neoplasm. All major WHO diagnostic criteria for ET are either met or strongly supported: sustained marked thrombocytosis (>450 × 10⁹/L), bone marrow morphology showing megakaryocyte dysplasia (a key differentiator from reactive thrombocytosis), abnormal platelet morphology on peripheral smear, and exclusion of other causes — notably, no evidence of autoimmune disease, no signs of chronic inflammation (low ferritin confirms true iron deficiency, not anemia of chronic disease), and no secondary triggers identified (e.g., infection, malignancy, splenectomy). The presence of erythromelalgia — a canonical microvascular symptom in ET — further strengthens the diagnosis. Iron deficiency is plausibly explained by acquired von Willebrand syndrome (AVWS), a well-documented complication of extreme thrombocytosis (>1000 × 10⁹/L is typical, but AVWS can occur at ≥700 × 10⁹/L), leading to mucosal bleeding and subsequent iron loss. While JAK2/CALR/MPL testing is pending, >85% of ET cases harbor one of these driver mutations; their absence would prompt re-evaluation, but does not negate the provisional diagnosis given the robust morphologic and clinical evidence. Serum EPO is needed to exclude PV (which requires low EPO), but isolated thrombocytosis + megakaryocyte dysplasia + erythromelalgia makes PV unlikely. LDH and VWF studies are supportive/confirmatory, not diagnostic prerequisites. Thus, ET remains the single most coherent, evidence-supported diagnosis.
